title: Esther 3:1–6
context: Some years after Esther became queen (2:16; compare 3:7), King Ahasuerus, often identified with Xerxes I of Persia, promotes Haman the son of Hammedatha the Agagite above all the princes (3:1). The king’s servants bow to Haman by royal command, but Mordecai refuses, and when pressed daily he tells them he is a Jew (3:2–4). Haman is enraged and, scorning to strike Mordecai alone, seeks to destroy all the Jews throughout the kingdom (3:5–6). The text does not state Mordecai’s reason for refusing beyond his identity as a Jew. Many readers connect the label “Agagite” with Agag king of Amalek (1 Samuel 15) and the Benjamite Kish named in Mordecai’s genealogy (2:5) with Saul’s father (1 Samuel 9:1), which would set this conflict against the older enmity of Exodus 17:14–16 and Deuteronomy 25:17–19; others hold that these links are uncertain. The book never names God, and this commentary does not read that silence as either absence or code. Both traditions read the scene as the setting in which God’s care for his people will be quietly at work.

verses.text: After these things King Ahasuerus promoted Haman the son of Hammedatha the Agagite, and advanced him, and set his seat above all the princes who were with him.
verses.arminianNotes: Haman’s sudden rise comes without explanation, right after Mordecai’s unrewarded loyalty in 2:21–23. Arminian readers note the irony without making it mechanical: human rulers promote and overlook freely and often unjustly, and the story will show God working faithfully amid real choices made by a careless king and an ambitious courtier.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers often see the placing of Haman next to Mordecai’s unrewarded service as the first move in a pattern of providential reversal, with God governing even the promotions of a foreign court (compare Daniel 2:21). Shared ground: both traditions note that the label “Agagite” is often linked with Agag of 1 Samuel 15, while some readers take it as uncertain, and that the book itself never names God.

verses.text: All the king’s servants who were in the king’s gate bowed down and paid homage to Haman, for the king had so commanded concerning him. But Mordecai didn’t bow down or pay him homage.
verses.arminianNotes: Mordecai alone refuses to bow or pay homage, though the king had commanded it. The text does not say why. Arminian readers often weigh several suggestions, such as an inherited enmity with Amalek or a refusal of honor that seemed to cross into worship, and they stress that Mordecai’s stand is a genuine, costly decision of conscience that carries real consequences.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise note that the reason is not given, and many hesitate to treat ordinary courtesy toward rulers as forbidden, since Israelites bowed to kings elsewhere (for example 1 Samuel 24:8). They read Mordecai’s refusal as rooted in his identity as a Jew (3:4). Shared ground: both traditions avoid inventing a motive the narrator withholds and read the refusal as the trigger the story then traces.

verses.text: Then the king’s servants who were in the king’s gate said to Mordecai, “Why do you disobey the king’s commandment?”
verses.arminianNotes: The servants challenge Mordecai directly: why disobey the king’s commandment? Arminian readers see a familiar biblical tension between loyalty to an earthly ruler and loyalty rooted in covenant identity, and they note that Mordecai is given repeated opportunity to comply, so his continued refusal is a deliberate stance rather than an oversight.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers often connect the scene with other exile narratives where faithful Jews face a royal demand (compare Daniel 3 and 6), while noting that Esther’s account is more reticent about religious motive than Daniel’s. Shared ground: both traditions hear the question as the narrator’s way of raising the stakes and agree that the text does not frame Mordecai’s act explicitly as an act of worship or idolatry refused.

verses.text: Now it came to pass, when they spoke daily to him, and he didn’t listen to them, that they told Haman, to see whether Mordecai’s reason would stand; for he had told them that he was a Jew.
verses.arminianNotes: Mordecai’s colleagues speak to him daily, then report him to see whether his reason would stand, for he had told them he was a Jew. Arminian readers note that Mordecai openly discloses his identity even as Esther still conceals hers (2:10, 2:20), and they see the courtiers’ choice to inform Haman as their own free act that sets the crisis in motion.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers observe that Mordecai’s identity as a Jew is the only reason the narrator records, which turns a personal slight into a matter concerning the whole people. They see God’s providence overruling even the informers’ curiosity without making it any less theirs. Shared ground: both traditions note the contrast between Mordecai’s openness here and Esther’s concealment, and that the text gives no further explanation.

verses.text: When Haman saw that Mordecai didn’t bow down nor pay him homage, Haman was full of wrath.
verses.arminianNotes: Haman sees for himself and is full of wrath. Arminian readers see wounded pride turning into rage, a moral portrait of how unchecked self-regard escalates, and they stress that Haman is fully responsible for what he does with his anger. The book invites readers to notice the danger of power joined to injured vanity.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise read Haman’s wrath as a revealing of his heart, and they often connect it with biblical warnings that pride goes before destruction (Proverbs 16:18). They hold that God permits and governs such wrath without approving it. Shared ground: both traditions treat Haman’s anger as his own sin, and both read the verse as preparing for the pattern of pride brought low later in the book.

verses.text: But he scorned the thought of laying hands on Mordecai alone, for they had made known to him Mordecai’s people. Therefore Haman sought to destroy all the Jews who were throughout the whole kingdom of Ahasuerus, even Mordecai’s people.
verses.arminianNotes: Scorning to strike Mordecai alone, Haman seeks to destroy all the Jews throughout the kingdom. Arminian readers stress the horror of a personal grievance becoming a plan to destroy a whole people, and they see a real moral choice at each step. They hold that God hates such malice and that the story will show him preserving his people without overriding human agency.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers read this as an attempt against the covenant people and so, in canonical perspective, against God’s promises to preserve the line of Abraham (compare Genesis 12:3). Many connect it with the enmity of Amalek, though they note that the link is inferred. Shared ground: both traditions take the threat of destruction with grave seriousness and see God’s faithfulness to his people at stake in it.
